parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German almuosen, from Old High German alamuosa, from Proto-West Germanic *alemōsinā, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “pitiful, merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē). The m

parole.significato: altar (table or similar structure used for religious rites)
parole.testo: From Middle High German alter, altære, from Old High German altāri, from Proto-West Germanic *altārī (“altar”), borrowed from Latin altāre. The form was readapted to the Latin source, partly to avoid homophony with Alter (“age”). Compare also Dutch altaar alongside archaic outer.
From Middle High German balsam, balsame, from Old High German balsamo, from Proto-West Germanic *balsamō. Doublet of Bisam and Desman.

parole.significato: to seal something, to set the seal on something.
parole.testo: From Middle High German besigelen, from Old High German bisigilen, from Proto-West Germanic *bisiglijan, from Latin sigillō (“to seal”). Equivalent to be- + siegeln.

From Middle High German beziehen, from Old High German biziohan, from Proto-West Germanic *biteuhan. Equivalent to be- + ziehen. The sense “to refer” is probably influenced by Latin referre. Compare Dutch betrekken.

From Middle High German bischof, from Old High German biscof, from Proto-West Germanic *biskop, from Latin episcopus. The -f- is due to the High German consonant shift, but in Middle High German it irregularly developed into -v- (thus predominantly bischoves rather than bischoffes), which explains t

From Middle High German brucke, from Old High German brugga, brucca, from Proto-West Germanic *bruggju. The neurological sense “pons” is a semantic loan from Latin pōns. Cognates Compare Bavarian Bruckn, Dutch brug, English bridge, Low German Brügg, Danish brygge, Old Saxon bruggia.
From Middle High German and Old High German buhs, from Proto-West Germanic *buhs, from Latin buxus. Cognate with Middle Dutch bos, English box.

From Middle High German buter, butter, from Old High German butera, from Proto-West Germanic *buterā (“butter”). Though originally feminine, the word became masculine throughout Upper German and in southern dialects of West Central German. The now established feminine gender is East Central German,
Inherited from Middle High German bühse. Doublet of Buchse (the Upper German form).

parole.significato: tub, vat, barrel (open vessel, often large and made of wood)
parole.testo: From Middle High German bütte, from Old High German *butta, from Proto-West Germanic *buttjā. Cognate with Yiddish ביט (bit).

From Middle High German dechant, techant, from Old High German tehhant, tehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *dekan (“deacon”), from Latin decanus (“dean”). Doublet of Dekan, a 15th-century borrowing. In Middle Low German dēken, the full vowel in the second syllable was protected by adaptation to variou

parole.significato: cathedral (church serving as seat of a bishop, by extension, any large church)
parole.testo: 15th-century alteration (see below) of older Thum, from Middle High German and Old High German tuom, from Proto-West Germanic *dōm (whence Old Dutch duom, Middle Low German dôm), from Medieval Latin domus (literally “house”). The use probably goes back to domus episcopatus/episcopalis (“house of the

From Middle High German trache, from Old High German trahho, from Proto-West Germanic *drakō, borrowed from Latin dracō. The modern initial d- is influenced by the original Latin, reinforced by dialectal German forms.

parole.significato: a plant of the genus Althaea
parole.testo: From Middle High German ībesche, from Old High German ībisca, from Proto-West Germanic *ībisku, from Late Latin ibīscum, hībiscum. Doublet of Hibiskus.

From Middle High German einhorn, einhurne, from Old High German einhorn(o), einhurn(o), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *ainahorn, a calque of Latin ūnicornis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek μονόκερως (monókerōs). Equivalent to ein + Horn.
From Middle High German esel, from Old High German esil, from late Proto-West Germanic *asil, which is borrowed from Late Latin asellus.

parole.significato: fall, drop (the act of falling or an instance thereof)
parole.testo: From Middle High German val, from Old High German fal, from Proto-West Germanic *fall. Cognate with Dutch val, English fall. The sense “case” in all its shapes is a calque of Latin casus.
From Middle High German fieber, from Old High German fiebar, from Proto-West Germanic *fēbr, borrowed from Latin febris (“fever”).
From Middle High German vlegel, from Old High German flegil, from Proto-West Germanic *flagil, probably from Latin flagellum.

From Middle High German vrītac, from Old High German frīatag (9th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *Frījā dag (“day of Frigg”), calque of Latin dies Veneris. Compare Low German Freedag, Dutch vrijdag, English Friday, Danish fredag.

parole.significato: a vault, tomb, masoned grave; any kind, but especially one that is underground
parole.testo: From Middle High German gruft, kruft, from Old High German gruft, kruft, chruft, from Proto-West Germanic *krufti, an early borrowing from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Cognate with Dutch krocht, Middle Low German kruft, Old English cruft. Doublet of Grotte and Krypta. Some autho

From Middle High German impfen (“to graft”), from Old High German impfōn (impitōn), from Proto-West Germanic *impōn, from Vulgar Latin *imputō (“to graft”) (unrelated to imputō (“to reckon, attribute”)), from Ancient Greek ἔμφυτος (émphutos, “planted”). Compare English imp.
From Middle High German ingewer, ingeber, from Old High German ingiber, gingiber, gingibero, from Proto-West Germanic *gingiberō.

From Middle High German insel, insele, isele, from Old High German isila, *insila, from Proto-West Germanic *isulā, *insulā, borrowed from Latin *isula, insula (“island”). Native Middle High German words for “island” were ouwe and wert; cf. modern Aue (“meadow by a river”) and Werder (“river island”

parole.significato: lime (general term for inorganic materials containing calcium)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kalc, from Old High German kalk, from Proto-West Germanic *kalk.
From Middle High German kamer, from Old High German kamara, from Proto-West Germanic *kamarā (“chamber”). Doublet of Kamera (“camera”) and Kamurke (“chamber”).
From Middle High German karte, from Old High German karta, from Proto-West Germanic *kardā, from Latin carduus.

parole.significato: dungeon (immured and very austere prison, often underground)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kerker, kerkære, karkære, from Old High German karkāri, karkari, karkeri, from Proto-West Germanic *karkarī, ultimately from Latin carcer. Doublet of Karzer (“arrest cell, especially at a university”), a later borrowing of the same noun.
From Middle High German kirse, from Old High German kirsa, from Proto-West Germanic *kirsijā, from Late Latin ceresia.
From Middle High German kiste, from Old High German kista, from Proto-West Germanic *kistu (“chest, box”).

parole.significato: cook (one who cooks; male or unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Middle High German koch, from Old High German choch, from Proto-West Germanic *kok (“a cook”).

From Middle High German kuofe (also küefe), from Old High German kuofa, of obscure origin. Perhaps from Proto-West Germanic *kōpā, *kōpu, from Late Latin *cō̆pa, a variant of Latin cūpa (“tub, vat, cask”), whence also Old Saxon kōpa, Middle Low German kôpe (“vat, tub, barrel”). Merged with Middle Hi
From Middle High German kupfer, from Old High German kupfar, from Proto-West Germanic *kopr (“copper”).

From Middle High German kurz, from Old High German kurz, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, from Latin curtus. Compare also native Old High German *skurz, scurz and Middle High German schurz. Cognate with Dutch and Low German kort, English curt, Swedish kort.
From Middle High German küche, from Old High German chuhhina, from late Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

parole.significato: a wall, usually one made of stone or concrete
parole.testo: From Middle High German mūre, from Old High German mūra, from Proto-West Germanic *mūrā, from Latin mūrus, from Proto-Italic *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey-. Cognate with Yiddish מויער (moyer).
From Middle High German mūlber(e), from Old High German mūlbere, a dissimilated variant of older mūrberi, from Proto-West Germanic *mūrubaʀi ~ *mōrubaʀi, from Latin mōrus.
From Middle High German meister, from Old High German meistar, from Proto-West Germanic *maistar (“master”). Doublet of Maestro, Magister, and Master.
From Middle High German pasternacke, from Old High German pastinaka, from Proto-West Germanic *pastinakā (“parsnip”).

Inherited from Middle High German pëch, bëch, from Old High German pëh, bëh, from Proto-West Germanic *pik (“pitch, tar, wood resin”), from Latin pix. The form is unusual as it shows unshifted p-, but shifted -ch, even though the shift of initial p- to pf- occurred later than that of postvocalic -k
From Middle High German pfāl, phāl, from Old High German pfāl, from Proto-West Germanic *pālu, from Latin pālus.

From Middle High German pfīl, from Old High German pfīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl, from Latin pīlum (“javelin, throwing spear”). Cognate with German Low German Piel, Dutch pijl (“arrow, dart”), English pile (“column of wood, steel or concrete”).

From Middle High German phert, phærît, pherit, pferift (“riding horse”), from Old High German pherit, pfarifrit, parafred, from Proto-West Germanic *parafred, from Late Latin paraverēdus (originally “substitute post horse”). Largely displaced the native word Ross. Compare Dutch paard and English pal
From Middle High German pforte, from Old High German pforta, from Proto-West Germanic *portā (“portal, gateway”), from Latin porta (“gateway, passage”).

parole.significato: to glue, to stick [with auf (+ accusative) ‘onto’]
parole.testo: From Middle High German bichen, pichen, picken (“to coat with pitch”), from Middle High German pech, bech (“pitch”), from Old High German peh, beh, from Proto-West Germanic *pik (“pitch, tar, wood resin”), from Latin pix (“pitch, tar”). Compare Pech.
From Middle High German rëgel, from Old High German rëgula, from Proto-West Germanic *regulu, from Latin regula (“rule”).

From Middle High German salbeie, salveie f, from Old High German salbeia, salveia f, from Proto-West Germanic *salbejā (“sage”), from Late Latin salvegia, from Latin salvia. Cognate with English sage.
From Middle High German sūber, from Old High German sūbar, from Proto-West Germanic *sūbrī, from Latin sobrius (“sober”).

From Middle High German scheide, from Old High German sceida, from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþiju. Compare Low German scheed, Dutch schede, English sheath, Danish skede, Norwegian Bokmål skjede, Icelandic skeið. The anatomical sense (16th c.) is a calque of Latin vagīna. The sense “partition” is atte

parole.significato: to write, to write out (use letters to make words and texts)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schrīben, from Old High German scrīban, from Proto-West Germanic *skrīban (“to write”), from Latin scrībō.
From Middle High German schrift, from Old High German scrift, from Proto-West Germanic *skrifti (“writing, scripture”), from Latin scriptum.

parole.significato: school (an institution dedicated to teaching and learning (especially before university); department/institute at a col…
parole.testo: From Middle High German schuole, from Old High German scuola.

parole.significato: coulter (knife on a plough, fixed in front of the ploughshare)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sech, from Old High German seh, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], derived from Latin secare (“to cut off”).
From Middle High German sīde, from Old High German sīda, from Proto-West Germanic *sīdā (“silk”), from sēta (“silk”), from Latin saeta (“horsehair; bristle; silk”).
From Middle High German semele, Old High German semala, from Proto-West Germanic *similā (“wheat flour”). Compare Yiddish זעמל (zeml).

Inherited from Middle High German senne, from Old High German senno, from Proto-West Germanic *sannjō (“herdsman, dairyman”), from Vulgar Latin saniō (“herdsman, dairyman”), deemed a borrowing from Celtic languages, the stem preserved in Old Irish sine (“nipple, teat”), reconstructing Proto-Celtic *

parole.significato: safe, secure (not dangerous or in danger)
parole.testo: From Middle High German siher, from Old High German sihur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur (“secure, sure”), from Latin sēcūrus (“worryless; carefree; secure”).
From Middle High German sigelen, from Old High German sigilen, from Proto-West Germanic *siglijan, from Latin sigillō (“to seal”).

parole.significato: Sunday (the first day of the week in many religious traditions, and the seventh day of the week in systems using the IS…
parole.testo: From Middle High German sunne(n)tac, sun(n)tac, from Old High German sunnūntag (9th c.), from late Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag (“day of the sun”), a calque of Latin diēs Sōlis (4th c.), equivalent to Sonne + Tag. Compare Low German Sünndag, Dutch zondag, West Frisian snein, English Sunday, Danis
From Middle High German spīcher, from Old High German spīhhāri, from Proto-West Germanic *spīkārī, borrowed from Late Latin spīcārium.
From Middle High German spīse, from Old High German spīsa, from Proto-West Germanic *spīsā, borrowed from Latin expēnsa (“expense”) (Late Latin form spēsa).

parole.significato: to donate, to give as charity
parole.testo: From Middle High German spenden, from Old High German spentōn (“to consume, use, spend”), from Proto-West Germanic *spendōn (“to spend”), from Latin expendō.

parole.significato: mirror (smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside, that reflects light)
parole.testo: From Middle High German spiegel, from Old High German spiegal, spēgal, from Proto-West Germanic *spēgl (“mirror”). Cognate with Hunsrik Spieghel.

parole.significato: street; road (a way wide enough to be passable for vehicles, generally paved, in or outside a settlement)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German strāȥe, from Old High German strāȥa, from Proto-West Germanic *strātu (“street”), from Latin (via) strata. Sense 6 (“strait”) is a calque of Middle Low German strâte, itself a phono-semantic matching of Middle English streit, from Old French estreit (“narrow”), from

parole.significato: the Devil, Satan (supreme evil spirit in the Abrahamic religions)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tiuvel, from Old High German tiufal, from Proto-West Germanic *diubul, from Latin diabolus, ultimately from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “false accuser, slanderer”). Cognate to Bavarian Teifl, Deife, Pennsylvania German Deiwel, Dutch duivel, Old Saxon diubol (German Low
From Middle High German trahten, from Old High German trahtōn, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtōn, from Latin tractāre (“to drag, manage, handle”). Doublet of traktieren.
Conflation of Middle High German elm, from Old High German elm, from Proto-West Germanic *elm (“elm”), and Latin ulmus (“elm”).
From Middle High German and Old High German wal, from Proto-West Germanic *wall, from Latin vallum. Cognate with English wall.
From Middle High German wī(h)er, from earlier wīwære, from Old High German wīwāri, from Proto-West Germanic *wīwārī (“pond”), from Latin vīvārium. Doublet of Vivarium.
